title: Dhanna the farmer
hookLine: Dhanna prays plainly for flour, lentils, ghee, a cow and a good wife (Dhanasri, Dhanna, ang 695)

lines: O GOPAL, A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR.
BETWEEN HYMNS OF THE SOUL, A LIST.
cards: O Gopal, I'm a beggar at Your door. That's how one hymn in the Guru Granth Sahib begins, in paraphrase, and what follows sounds less like poetry than a shopping list. It sits between hymns about the soul and the Infinite.
It belongs to Dhanna, a farmer, and it's addressed straight to God. He doesn't dress it up or explain himself. He stands at the door and asks for groceries.

teach.h: A BEGGAR AT YOUR DOOR, GOPAL.
teach.b: The hymn is in Raag Dhanasri, on Ang 695. It opens with the word aarta. Some read it as one in need, a beggar at the door; others hear in it aarti, an offering of worship.
In paraphrase: O Gopal, Sustainer of the world, I'm a beggar at Your door; You take care of the work of those devoted to You. Then the list.

teach.h: LENTILS, FLOUR, GHEE, SHOES, A COW.
teach.b: Lentils, flour and ghee, so my heart can be content each day. Shoes, and good clothes. Grain.
A cow and a buffalo that give milk. A fine horse. And a good wife to keep the home.
The last line: your servant Dhanna asks for these. No apology, no explanation that what he really wants is something higher.
Look at the kind of things they are: food for the table, something on the feet, animals that keep a farm alive, a partner.
It's the list of a working household, said out loud to the Lord, as if the Lord were the one who could be asked.
And it stands in the Guru's book, beside songs of longing for the Lord. Some people feel a prayer has to be cleaned up first: made noble, made about other people, the part about rent hidden.

Dhanna's hymn quietly says the plain thing is allowed. Trust shows up in the asking. Tradition tells other stories about Dhanna, about a stone and a simple farmer's faith; those can wait for another day.
Today it's the list, and the man who wasn't embarrassed to say it to God.

how: Dhanna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikhs bring ordinary needs as well as spiritual ones into ardas, the standing prayer.

o: one in need at the Lord's door, or an offering
a hymn sung only at weddings and festivals
a list of rules for a farmer's household

p: so the heart is content each day
the last thing on the list

s: Dhanna asks only for spiritual gifts
he asks for lentils, flour, ghee, shoes, clothes, a cow, a horse and a good wife.
the hymn sits in the Guru Granth Sahib
Dhanna apologizes for asking for ordinary things
there's no apology; the hymn ends simply: your servant Dhanna asks for these.

games.q: you're Dhanna, a farmer, standing before the Lord with real needs at home. what do you say?
o: name the groceries, the cow and the shoes, plainly.
say nothing, so as not to bother God.
games.why: he names them all, plainly, as a beggar at the door, and the hymn sits in the Guru's book.

practice: Find your most ordinary need, not the noblest: groceries for the week, a night of sleep, a car that starts, a kind word at work.
If you pray, offer it plainly, as Dhanna did, someone asking at a door; if you don't, simply hold it honestly as a need. Then let it go out with the breath, with Waheguru if you like.

wordCard.voice: Aarta. The word that opens Dhanna's hymn, read as a beggar at the door or as an offering of worship: lentils, flour, ghee, shoes, a cow, a wife, asked for plainly.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the hymn's opening (Ang 695). aarta is read by some as 'one in need at Your door', by others as 'Your aarti'.

carryVoice: Your line: plain prayers count. Lentils and flour made it into the Guru's book. See you tomorrow.
